title: The first census
unit: men twenty and older able to serve
summary: Numbered in the Wilderness of Sinai in the second year after the Exodus. Levi is left out (1:47–49), and Joseph is counted as two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, so there are still twelve. The twelve figures add up exactly to the 603,550 of 1:46, and the same total is given for the tabernacle's silver in Exodus 38:26. Every figure but Gad's (45,650) is a round hundred. How large the numbers are is debated: 'thousand' translates the Hebrew ʾeleph, which some scholars read here as a clan or military unit rather than a thousand.

sources.note: the same 603,550, each paying half a shekel

title: The second census
unit: men twenty and older able to serve
summary: Numbered on the plains of Moab at the end of the wilderness years: not one man from the first census was left except Caleb and Joshua (26:64–65). The total barely moves, 1,820 fewer than the 603,550 of Numbers 1, but the tribes do. Simeon falls by 37,100 to 22,200, from the third largest to the smallest; Manasseh grows by 20,500 and now comes before Ephraim, which fell by 8,000. The text does not say why Simeon shrank. The plague at Peor had just killed 24,000 (25:9) and the man at its centre was a Simeonite chief (25:14), and readers often connect the two, but that is an inference. The Levites are counted apart again, 23,000 males a month old or more (26:62).

title: The camp round the tabernacle
unit: men twenty and older able to serve
summary: The twelve figures of the census in Numbers 1, unchanged, arranged into four camps of three tribes, one on each side of the Tent of Meeting, with the Levites camped round the tent in the middle (2:2, 2:17). Each camp has its own total and marches in its own turn: Judah's camp on the east, the largest at 186,400, sets out first (2:9); Reuben's on the south second; Ephraim's on the west, the smallest at 108,100, third; Dan's on the north last. The four totals add up to the 603,550 of 2:32. The order of the list follows the camps rather than Numbers 1: Judah, Issachar and Zebulun, fourth to sixth in the census, now come first.

sources.note: the same twelve figures in the census

title: The Levites counted apart
unit: Levite males a month old or more
summary: The Levites were left out of the census of fighting men (1:47–49) and counted here instead, every male from a month old, clan by clan, each with its place round the tabernacle: Gershon behind it on the west (3:23), Kohath on the south (3:29), Merari on the north (3:35), and Moses, Aaron and Aaron's sons on the east before the entrance (3:38). The three clans add up to 22,300, but the total in 3:39 is 22,000. The BSB notes that some Septuagint manuscripts read Kohath as 8,300, which gives 22,000. The 22,000 is the figure the text goes on to use: the Levites redeem 22,000 of Israel's 22,273 firstborn, and the other 273 are bought back at five shekels each (3:43–48).
discrepancy: the text's total is 300 fewer. The BSB notes that some Septuagint manuscripts read Kohath as 8,300 (3:28), which gives 22,000

title: The first return from Babylon
summary: The families and towns of those who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, each with its number: the men of Israel by family and by town (2:3–35), then the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants, and those who could not prove their descent. The text's total is 42,360 (2:64), besides 7,337 servants and 200 singers (2:65). But the figures listed add up to only 29,818. Nehemiah 7 copies the same list, with many figures a little different, and its figures add up to 31,089, against the same 42,360; the Greek 1 Esdras gives 30,143. Keil takes the differences for copying errors in long lists of numbers. Older interpreters, Jewish and Christian, took the total to include returnees of the other tribes whose families are not listed. The chart shows the gap either way.
discrepancy: the text's total is 12,542 more. Keil takes the differences for copying errors; older interpreters (Seder Olam, Rashi, Ussher) took the total to include returnees of other tribes not listed by family

title: The list of the first return, as Nehemiah found it
summary: Nehemiah found 'the genealogical record of those who had first returned' (7:5) and copies it: the same list as Ezra 2, family by family, with the same total of 42,360 (7:66). Behind each bar is Ezra's figure for the same family. Seventeen of the 39 figures the two lists share differ, most by a few, some by hundreds or more: Arah 652 against 775, Azgad 2,322 against 1,222, Senaah 3,930 against 3,630. A few names differ too (Hariph for Jorah, Gibeon for Gibbar), Bethlehem and Netophah are counted together, and Magbish is missing. The figures here add up to 31,089, 1,271 more than Ezra's, and both fall short of the total they share. Keil takes the differences for copying errors in the transmission of long lists of numbers.
discrepancy: the text's total is 11,271 more, as Ezra's is (Ezra 2:64). Keil takes the differences for copying errors; older interpreters took the total to include returnees of other tribes not listed by family

title: The 144,000 sealed
summary: John hears the number of those sealed, 144,000 from all the tribes of Israel (7:4), and then the tribes one by one, 12,000 each: a list whose bars are all the same length, unlike every census in Numbers. The list is not any of the Old Testament's. It begins with Judah, not Reuben the firstborn; it counts Levi, whom the censuses leave out; it names Joseph and Manasseh but not Ephraim; and it leaves out Dan. The text gives no reason for any of it. Irenaeus took Dan's absence to mean that the Antichrist would come from Dan, reading Jeremiah 8:16 ('the snorting of his horses is heard from Dan'); that is one reading, not the text's. The 144,000 appear again in 14:1, standing with the Lamb on Mount Zion.

title: David's twelve monthly divisions
summary: The army served in turn, one division a month, 'and there were 24,000 men in each division' (27:1): twelve commanders, each named with his month, most of them from the lists of David's mighty men (11:10-47). The chart is flat on purpose: every division is the same size, a rota rather than a census. The text gives no total; twelve divisions of 24,000 make 288,000, a sum Keil sets beside Joab's census of the whole nation (2 Sam 24:9; 1 Chr 21:5) as the army in service against the men able to bear arms. The same chapter says the census itself 'was not entered in the Book of the Chronicles of King David' (27:24).

title: David's census, as Samuel tells it
summary: Joab takes nine months and twenty days to count the fighting men from Dan to Beersheba (24:8), and reports 800,000 in Israel and 500,000 in Judah (24:9), 1,300,000 together, though the text gives no total. Chronicles tells the same census with other figures (1 Chr 21:5), and its chart draws these behind its own. The census was never entered in the royal annals (1 Chr 27:24); Keil takes the figures for round numbers handed down by word of mouth, which is why the two accounts differ.

title: David's census, as Chronicles tells it
summary: Chronicles gives Joab's report as 1,100,000 men in all Israel and 470,000 in Judah (21:5), where Samuel has 800,000 in Israel and 500,000 in Judah (2 Sam 24:9). Behind Judah's bar is Samuel's figure: 30,000 fewer here. The two Israel figures are not drawn against each other, because they may not count the same thing: the BSB reads Judah's 470,000 as included in all Israel's 1,100,000, which leaves 630,000 for the rest of Israel against Samuel's 800,000, while Keil reads them as two figures, 1,570,000 together against Samuel's 1,300,000. Chronicles adds that Joab did not count Levi or Benjamin, 'because the king's command was detestable to him' (21:6). The census was never entered in the royal annals (27:24), and Keil takes both accounts' figures for round numbers handed down by word of mouth.
